source.title: Escaping Plato's Cave: JAM for Aligning Independently Trained Vision and Language Models
source.authors: L. H. Yoon; Yi-Song Yue; Been Kim

record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares cross-modal alignment measurements across matched and hard-nonmatch inputs and different similarity metrics, but it does not reproduce the full Platonic Representation Hypothesis evaluation.
record.gate_note: Tables 7 and 9 report the study's own CKA and CKNNA alignment scores for matched and hard-nonmatch image-caption pairs. The authors state that hard nonmatches can score nearly as highly as matches. Table 4 reports retrieval after JAM has been trained to align the representations; this is not a direct measurement of whether unmodified representations' distances converge with scale, so those rows are recorded under fits_no_version. Other trained JAM retrieval results are omitted because alignment is induced by the training objective and they do not directly measure a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The unmodified-backbone experiments directly qualify statistical evidence for convergence: alignment metrics distinguish matches from easy controls but largely miss fine-grained mismatches. This bears on V6. The JAM experiments deliberately induce alignment and do not establish spontaneous convergence or interchangeability with little loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the statistical-metric and scaling discussions but omits the principal conclusion: the authors argue that supervised post-hoc joint autoencoding of frozen unimodal backbones produces useful cross-modal coherence and competitive specialist retrieval. They interpret hard-negative score similarity as a limitation of metric granularity, explicitly preserving their interpretation of real coarse alignment. Their reported scaling plateau concerns JAM retrieval in a small-data regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies CKNNA, a metric cited from the Platonic Representation Hypothesis work, alongside CKA and other metrics on SugarCrepe image-caption pairs. It adds a fine-grained hard-negative comparison rather than reproducing the original study's full evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported alignment depends on which image-caption pairs are compared: hard nonmatches retain scores close to matches. CKA and CKNNA are distinct metrics; CKNNA uses k nearest neighbors = 10.

fits_no_version.finding: JAM-trained retrieval shows no consistent ordering by language-model parameter count with DINOv2 ViT-L fixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter count does not consistently predict fine-grained retrieval after supervised JAM alignment in this small-data setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear projection with Spread reaches 85.95, 91.94, and 63.33 binary Recall@1, versus JAM's 88.01, 95.74, and 80.20 on Replace, Add, and Swap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised linear projection can align frozen image and text embeddings for retrieval, but its performance depends on task and adaptation architecture.

record.problems: The statistical alignment tables report no uncertainty estimates. Table 4 tests only three different language-model families/sizes with one fixed vision backbone; retrieval follows deliberate JAM alignment training and is not a direct measure of innate representational convergence. The reported statistical comparisons use k = 10 for CKNNA, with no sweep over that setting.
record.rows_left_out: Included CKA and CKNNA rows for Replace and Swap tasks. Omitted Table 8 (Add task) and the SVCCA and CCA measurements from Tables 7 and 9 to stay within the 60-row limit; these are additional task/metric results of the same type. JAM retrieval results outside Table 4 were omitted because they likewise follow deliberately induced alignment and do not directly test a listed version.

untested.parts: Increasing spontaneous alignment with model size or capability across independently trained systems.
Increasing cross-modal alignment as both unimodal models improve; statistical tests use fixed backbones and scaling results follow alignment training.
Shared features or subspaces across independent initializations of the same architecture.
Representation interchangeability with little loss through simple mappings, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired alignment.
Recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.

A controlled nearest-neighbor-setting sweep, out-of-distribution generalization, and whether scale-related convergence trends disappear under alternative metrics. Kernel variants are reported, but no systematic robustness sweep is provided.
Incomplete or plateauing spontaneous convergence and causal explanations involving shared pretraining data or objectives.

missing.what: Easy-nonmatch CKA/CKNNA controls for Replace: Gemma2–DINOv2 0.020/0.006; Llama3.2–DINOv2 0.027/0.010; OLMo2–DINOv2 0.028/0.008; Gemma2–ResNet50 0.028/0.006. These establish the coarse-versus-fine distinction underlying the V6 verdict.

Easy-nonmatch CKA/CKNNA controls for Swap: Gemma2–DINOv2 0.037/0.014; Llama3.2–DINOv2 0.049/0.012; OLMo2–DINOv2 0.050/0.012; Gemma2–ResNet50 0.029/0.014. The table does not separate the two described easy-control constructions.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted numerical values agree with the supplied tables. Observed states for A rows refer to the V6 metric limitation demonstrated by paired comparisons, not complete representational convergence. Appendix B.3 states feature dimension 10 for CKA and CKNNA; this preprocessing condition should accompany the rows. Different metrics' numerical magnitudes alone do not establish contradictory convergence conclusions. No uncertainty or significance tests accompany the statistical tables. Declared omissions of Add, CCA, and SVCCA results are not repeated as missing.

versions.untested_parts: The Table 4 scale experiment measures retrieval after deliberately training JAM, not whether independently trained models' unmodified representational distances become more alike as size and capability rise.
The study evaluates paired image-caption alignment, but does not test whether alignment rises as both the vision and language models become better.
No comparison of independently initialized seeds of the same architecture for shared features or subspaces.

JAM trains modality-specific autoencoders jointly for alignment; the study does not test interchangeable representations with little loss, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
No test of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
The reported metric and input comparisons concern SugarCrepe Replace and Swap tasks. No out-of-distribution comparison or sweep over metric settings such as different k values is reported.
The study does not test whether alignment plateaus or whether shared pretraining data or objectives explain alignment.

relationships.condition: SugarCrepe Replace and Swap; frozen unimodal backbones; CKA and CKNNA with k=10
relationships.reason: A01–A32 show that fine-grained mismatches preserve nearly matching scores; CKA even increases for Gemma2–DINOv2 while CKNNA decreases. Missing easy-control rows show much lower scores. This supports dependence on metric and semantic granularity, without establishing that convergence vanishes.
relationships.display_finding: Fine-grained mismatches preserved nearly matching scores and increased Gemma2–DINOv2 CKA while decreasing CKNNA; easy controls produced much lower scores.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SugarCrepe Replace and Swap matched versus hard-nonmatch pairs; reported CKA and CKNNA scores
reader_labels.reason: Hard-nonmatch scores remain close to matched-pair scores, and some are identical at the reported precision, consistent with the authors' statement that hard nonmatches can be nearly indistinguishable from matches; see rows A01-A32.
